title: Kenzo Tsushima of Morae on Innovation, Change Management, and Servant Leadership
author: Kenzo Tsushima

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source reports rapid feature expansion and predicts broader competitive shifts, but does not address whether those products achieve sustained adoption, workflow fit, renewal value or other realized benefits. Its unmeasured claim that products are now viable competitors is therefore insufficient to support or oppose the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: In other words, they’ve really innovated and built in full feature sets, which means that they’re now genuinely viable competitors to the incumbents in the market.
We think we’ll see that in quite a few more categories.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Shaver’s comments show that legal-technology competition can shift quickly and encourage following competitive analyses, but they do not address the cluster’s central preference for selective filtering, contextual learning and organisational knowledge over chasing releases.

Those of you interested in having a look at our competitive analysis for contract review,  and following along for new competitive analysis releases, please check out Make sure to follow along in our newsletters as well so you don’t miss anything in the future.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Tsushima supports a bounded, human-supervised view of legal AI and rejects wholesale lawyer replacement, but the supplied evidence does not address apprenticeship, junior-work removal, leverage, training investment or partner succession. It therefore does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal expertise-pipeline proposition.
qs: Either the use cases are so narrow and there’s not a lot of creativity on how to deploy it more enterprise-wide, or it’s so overbroad that people are like, I’m gonna lose my job because it can do everything I’ve been doing as an attorney for 20 years.
So I am a firm believer that we need humans in the loop.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The supplied excerpts only direct listeners to Tsushima’s contact channels and Morae’s practice resources. They provide no substantive argument or evidence about whether legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation and human control.
qs: Kenzo Tsushima (39:03)  Sure, so you can find me on LinkedIn.
So that’s a really easy way to find the solutions we’re doing.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Tsushima supports the cluster’s principal proposition by advocating client-first deployment, broader but human-supervised AI use, and sustained change management rather than tool acquisition alone. He also identifies historically profitable billing models as a barrier to law-firm redesign, but offers practitioner observations rather than measured evidence on productivity, employment or apprenticeship.
qs: And I think everyone needs to go back into a mentality of client first and then product after.
So now with something that’s way past, you know, any sort of CLM and we’re talking really quick processing of information, the change management is probably the most important part.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Tsushima aligns with the cluster’s use-case-led view: LLMs expand document-intensive legal capabilities, but adoption should focus on specific workflows and demonstrated results rather than hype. He offers no measured evidence on performance and does not materially address human verification or the durability of specialist workflow layers.
qs: We needed to have specific use cases or specific targeted industries or specific workflows to make sure that…  it’s you’re not taking this for granted sight unseen, like, oh, I believe the AI is going to do a good job.
So if you have sets of documents or single documents or long form documents, you can query them and it can give you answers very quickly and it can synthesize that information.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Tsushima supports the cluster’s core view that AI value depends on client-led workflow design and organisational deployment rather than product access alone. He also aligns with its calibrated copilot model: AI should not replace experienced lawyers wholesale, but human oversight need not be continuous for every action.
qs: And I think everyone needs to go back into a mentality of client first and then product after.
The humans just don’t have to be in the loop 100 % of the time, right?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Tsushima aligns with the synthesis that AI will reshape legal-service production and commercial models without replacing experienced lawyers wholesale. He supports broader workflow redesign, client-led implementation and proportionate human oversight, while identifying entrenched billing models as a major barrier to change.
qs: Either the use cases are so narrow and there’s not a lot of creativity on how to deploy it more enterprise-wide, or it’s so overbroad that people are like, I’m gonna lose my job because it can do everything I’ve been doing as an attorney for 20 years.

What is still a struggle is getting a lot of law firms to think creatively about their billing models because it has been so historically effective, profitable, and just it’s been fantastic in terms of the US legal market, right?

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Tsushima directly supports the cluster’s framing of legal AI as organizational change rather than a software purchase. He makes change management central, links resistance to professional identity and perceived value, and advocates client-led workflow diagnosis and manageable experimentation. His productivity and career-security claims are anecdotal or predictive, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: So now with something that’s way past, you know, any sort of CLM and we’re talking really quick processing of information, the change management is probably the most important part.
In fact, we’ve glorified working 12 hours a day for so many years, you are so nervous about going down to eight hours a day because you don’t think you’re gonna be value add anymore.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of a fast-changing, increasingly competitive legal-AI market by describing challengers becoming viable through rapid feature development and anticipating similar shifts across additional categories. Its reference to competitive analysis also aligns with the need for current market intelligence, although it provides no adoption, revenue or comparative-performance evidence.
qs: In other words, they’ve really innovated and built in full feature sets, which means that they’re now genuinely viable competitors to the incumbents in the market.
We think we’ll see that in quite a few more categories.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Tsushima accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment: AI can generate substantial workflow-specific efficiencies but does not replace strategy, nuance or judgment. He likewise treats trust, secure architecture, workflow fit and change management—not tool access alone—as decisive for realised value. His support rests mainly on practitioner experience and company examples rather than controlled evidence.
qs: There are certain things that humans are just better at maybe AI in 30 years will be better at I don’t know, but there are just certain intuitive things where yeah, I need a person to do this This requires strategy this requires nuance  This requires the human in the loop and you can do both of those at the same time.
So now with something that’s way past, you know, any sort of CLM and we’re talking really quick processing of information, the change management is probably the most important part.

kp.k: Legal AI adoption is moving beyond observation
kp.d: Tsushima describes a shift from hype and watching in 2023–2024 toward active implementation in 2025, based on his impressions of Legal Week rather than a systematic adoption study. He predicts legal AI will be easier to establish than medical AI because medical data aggregation faces additional HIPAA and patient-data regulatory hurdles, while acknowledging legal ethics and standards of care.
qs: In 2024 and even in, sort of in 2023, we had the hype, we had a lot of people waiting on the sidelines, we had a lot of observation and now people want to do something and it was really reflective during that week.
it’s just going to be easier to stand up legal instances of AI before the medical instances just because of those bureaucratic hurdles.

kp.k: Workflow-specific applications address technology choice overload
kp.d: Tsushima says Morae launched its MorAI suite around June of the preceding year to translate proliferating technology into specific workflows and demonstrable use cases. He identifies document interrogation, synthesis, contracts and redlines as applications, emphasizing that customers should see results rather than accept assurances about AI performance.
qs: We needed to have specific use cases or specific targeted industries or specific workflows
you need to know because you need to see it with your own eyes.
if you have sets of documents or single documents or long form documents, you can query them and it can give you answers very quickly and it can synthesize that information.

kp.k: RFP reuse connects legal and procurement productivity
kp.d: Tsushima reports that Morae's Helpdesk module queries previous RFP responses to generate natural-language material for new responses, reducing manual copying and information retrieval. He claims internal and client time savings across legal and procurement workflows, but supplies no quantified hours, sample sizes or measured comparison.
qs: what if you just loaded your previous RFP responses into a MorAI tool, queried it and could get instant natural language output that you can just put in the RFP response, right?
it’s changed not only their legal process flow, but their procurement process flow. So you have two separate departments who are realizing the time and efficiency savings.

kp.k: Consulting-led implementation prioritizes client needs over product sales
kp.d: Tsushima positions Morae as an ALSP with a professional-services and consulting foundation, not simply a software seller. He argues that established advisory relationships support workflow discovery and that assessing the client's environment should precede product selection, including recommending another solution when MorAI does not fit.
qs: although we’re a tech company, a legal tech company, we’re not just a software company, right? We have at our core a professional services background.
even if we’re not providing the end technology for you, we’re going to point you in the right direction
everyone needs to go back into a mentality of client first and then product after.

kp.k: Selective human review supports AI-assisted legal work
kp.d: Tsushima rejects both excessively narrow conceptions of AI applications and expectations that AI can replace everything an experienced attorney does. He advocates human involvement without continuous review. As a personal anecdote, he reports using an NDA validator to identify mutuality and signing concerns, checking a flagged section and giving the document a cursory glance; he says this takes three minutes instead of 20. This is a reported workflow saving, not evidence establishing review accuracy or adequacy.
qs: I am a firm believer that we need humans in the loop. The humans just don’t have to be in the loop 100 % of the time
So I’ll look at section 5.3, but really I can give it a cursory glance and get it out the door. It takes me three minutes as opposed to 20 minutes
we have a standard of care and we have a legal responsibility to be the best stewards of the law and transactional law and process

kp.k: Change management addresses professional insecurity and retention
kp.d: Tsushima presents change management as central to adoption because lawyers may equate long hours with value and fear displacement. He recommends becoming an AI champion as a way to strengthen organizational standing. He illustrates potential benefits with a reduction from 12-hour to eight-hour days and asserts that adoption can lower attrition, churn and training costs, while acknowledging that these ancillary financial effects are difficult to track; no supporting retention dataset is provided.
qs: what is the quickest way to protect your own standing within your organization? Jump on board, become an AI champion.
the change management is probably the most important part.
we’ve glorified working 12 hours a day for so many years, you are so nervous about going down to eight hours a day because you don’t think you’re gonna be value add anymore.
there’s all these ancillary financial metrics that are a little bit hard to track because they’re soft.

kp.k: Data architecture and trust condition adoption
kp.d: Tsushima argues that provider size is not a sufficient basis for trusting an AI system and recommends understanding its underlying architecture. He describes MorAI Legal Companion as a private Azure instance using five LLMs, with legally specific training and separation of client data from other clients' models. These are the provider representative's security assertions, not an independently documented security assessment. He links uncertainty about privacy to reluctance to experiment and unused licenses.
qs: our flagship AI platform, MorAI Legal Companion, it’s a private Azure instance.
We’re not using this client’s data to train other clients’ models, et cetera. So we’re never co-mingling data.
our software uses five different LLMs, those are locked down to specifically legally trained instances.
if you’re afraid to prompt it in a certain way or to ask certain questions, you just won’t have the adoption.

kp.k: Multiple models reduce dependence on one development roadmap
kp.d: Tsushima explains Morae's multi-model strategy as a response to uneven development cycles among foundation-model providers. He says recommended models can change as relative capabilities improve, allowing workflows and adoption to evolve instead of remaining tied to one provider. His examples of switching between OpenAI and Anthropic are illustrative, not reported benchmark results.
qs: The development cycles for the underlying LLMs are not parallel.
if you leverage a lot of different LLMs that you can essentially substitute for one another and move up the priority level as they develop, you’re never locked into a single development cycle.
We want the legal use cases and the workflow developments and the actual adoption to evolve with the technology as well.

kp.k: ALSP training shifts staffing toward technology-enabled managed services
kp.d: Tsushima describes SEEDS, the Skill Enablement Employee Development Series, as training Morae lawyers in consulting and technology rather than assuming experienced practitioners can independently acquire these capabilities. He frames this as differentiation from legal staffing: attorneys should optimize client departments, use AI and teach client teams, rather than simply extend labor capacity. He reports improvements in public speaking and service delivery without quantitative outcome measures.
qs: really focusing on two things, consulting and technology.
they’re expected to automatically upskill themselves to now be a consultant and technologist
it is a tech enabled managed service where we’re staffing attorneys who know how to use AI platforms rather than just again, an extension of labor.
we’re going to consult on what optimal looks like in your legal department. So it’s never stagnant.

kp.k: Small experiments lower barriers to professional development
kp.d: Tsushima estimates internal reactions at approximately 80% excitement and 20% hesitation, explicitly presenting this as a high-level impression. He recommends 20-minute, achievable experiments—obtaining a login, uploading one contract and querying it—to let hesitant staff experience success before changing broader work habits. He acknowledges persistent resistance and concentrates encouragement on open-minded participants.
qs: I think we probably have 80 % excitement within our organization and 20 % hesitation
take 20 minutes today. get yourself a login to this tool, try the tool, throw in one legal contract here and query it.
some people are just never gonna get on board. So we try folks who are open-minded.

kp.k: New technical roles accompany resistance to billing change
kp.d: Tsushima reports emerging demand for legal engineers and prompt-engineering skills across firms, corporate legal departments and ALSPs. He characterizes legal engineering as uncommon a year and a half earlier but now a sought-after role. He also argues that historically profitable billing models and long-established managing partners make commercial change difficult, even where firms welcome AI for knowledge management and procurement. He does not specify a replacement pricing model.
qs: What is still a struggle is getting a lot of law firms to think creatively about their billing models
a year and a half ago, a legal engineer was not a common job.
Now it is a hot job. You want to be a legal engineer and that is a discipline that is sought out by old and young alike.
prompt engineering is kind of a mixture of art and science

kp.k: Servant leadership makes technology adoption concrete
kp.d: Tsushima advocates leaders demonstrating implementation and providing practical help instead of issuing mandates. He recounts spending 45 minutes building a model from Morae's latest statement-of-work template and distributing it to sales staff, who began using it. He presents this hands-on support as a way to reduce fear of technological obsolescence and build credibility.
qs: folks need to see you doing some of the dirty work.
I took 45 minutes, I built a new model based off of our latest SOW template and I disseminated it to our sales team and they loved it. They started using it already.
the tools to succeed rather than just telling you what to do. It has a much more positive effect on our workforce.

kp.k: Hiring discipline should not become automatic AI substitution
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about Shopify's CEO letter, Tsushima supports disciplined hiring forecasts but opposes rigid requirements to justify every person against AI. Drawing on pandemic hiring and subsequent layoffs as a cross-industry analogy, he emphasizes livelihoods, human strategy and nuance, and warns that excessive business-case requirements can impede operations. His preferred approach combines people with productivity-enhancing technology.
qs: these aren’t just numbers at the end of the day these are people’s lives and you have to respect that
You can’t be so rigid to be like you need to make a business case for personnel every single time and say why AI couldn’t do that
This requires strategy this requires nuance
You can make sure that human in the loop is leveraging technology to make them better, faster, stronger

kp.k: Buy rather than build; avoid selection paralysis
kp.d: Looking ahead, Tsushima treats adoption as inevitable and investment allocation as the central question. He recommends that firms and corporate legal departments buy platforms rather than build from scratch, acknowledging disagreement with that position. He identifies decision fatigue as an ongoing problem in mid 2025 and suggests choosing a readily deployable, slightly inferior option rather than delaying indefinitely; his 5% performance-gap example is hypothetical.
qs: I know a lot of people disagree
I always say, even if it’s not with us, please don’t build from scratch because you’re a law firm or you’re a corporate legal department. Focus on your business.
I continue to see it a lot in mid 2025, is there’s decision fatigue
if there’s a 5 % difference between the third best technology and the first best technology, just go with the third best one if it’s right in front of you and it’s easier to stand up and try it

kp.k: Restrictive AI policies may undermine junior retention
kp.d: Tsushima predicts that prohibiting workplace use of tools familiar from personal life will frustrate employees, particularly younger attorneys, and encourage departures to more permissive employers. He recommends enabling the emerging workforce rather than expecting it to accept historical working arrangements. This is a forward-looking retention argument, not a measured finding about junior attrition.
qs: you’re not allowed to use that here, that’s gonna cause a lot of frustration and they’re going to look elsewhere
if a law firm wants to have a good attrition rate, they need to make sure that their junior attorneys are engaging in the tools that they grew up with and that they know how to use.
we need to make sure that we’re setting them up for success so that they don’t just jump ship.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tsushima presents AI as a productivity and service-delivery tool whose adoption is becoming unavoidable, while Shaver reports rapid competitive change in contract-review technology.
pts.d: Kenzo Tsushima claims that legal AI is moving from the observation and hype of 2023–2024 toward implementation. He expects legal deployment to proceed more easily than medical deployment because of the latter's patient-data and regulatory hurdles. He describes document interrogation, synthesis, contract redlining, reuse of prior RFP responses, NDA review and SOW generation as practical applications. His NDA example retains selective human verification rather than replacing the lawyer entirely. He argues that AI adoption can improve work-life balance, reduce attrition and associated churn and training costs, and help employees protect their organizational standing. He says legal engineering and prompt-engineering skills are becoming more important, and describes Morae's move toward AI-enabled managed services rather than simply supplying additional legal labor. He identifies established law-firm billing models as an obstacle to change. He argues that multiple underlying LLMs allow providers and clients to benefit from different developers' improvements rather than remain tied to one model's development cycle. He recommends buying rather than building platforms from scratch and predicts that restrictions on familiar AI tools will frustrate younger lawyers and encourage departures. Separately, Nikki Shaver reports that emerging contract-review vendors have become viable competitors to incumbents in less than a year and expects similar changes in other legal-technology categories; her statement concerns the contract-review technology market and does not isolate AI as the cause.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The interview primarily supplies practitioner experience, internal deployment anecdotes and qualitative observations; Shaver refers to a comparative market-report process.
pts.d: Tsushima bases his claims on his experience leading Morae's consulting, AI and development work, client conversations and conference observations. For RFP workflows, he reports hours saved internally and positive client reactions but supplies no measured totals, sample sizes or comparative study. His NDA example gives a personal estimate of three minutes rather than twenty, with a cursory review of the AI-identified provision, not an accuracy benchmark or a demonstrated general reduction across legal tasks. His SOW example reports spending 45 minutes building a template-based model that the sales team immediately used. He estimates internal sentiment at 80% excitement and 20% hesitation, without describing a survey. Reduced attrition, shorter working days and ancillary financial savings are asserted or illustrated without reported retention data or financial calculations; he acknowledges the difficulty of tracking softer metrics. His claims that technology-oriented lawyers adopt more readily and that AI champions protect their jobs are experiential judgments, not labor-market findings. Morae's private Azure deployment, separation of client data and use of five legally focused LLMs are descriptions by its own executive, without an independent security audit or model-performance evaluation in the transcript. Shaver describes Legal Technology Hub's comparisons of feature completeness, market maturity and stability, referring to a July 2024 draft; the transcript does not reproduce the report's scores or underlying data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes ongoing changes in 2025 and near-term challenges, with benefits contingent on adoption, suitable workflows, training, trust and continued human involvement.
pts.d: Tsushima contrasts current implementation with the hype of 2023–2024 and tentatively dates the MorAI suite's launch to June of the preceding year, implying June 2024 in this 2025 interview. His observations about legal engineering and prompt engineering look back approximately eighteen months and two years respectively. He explicitly situates decision fatigue in mid-2025; the closing predictions respond to a question about the next couple of years rather than establish a precise deadline. His April-to-June 2025 model-switching example illustrates how a multi-LLM platform could accommodate improvements, not a verified forecast of which model would lead. Productivity and retention benefits depend on people actually adopting the tools, on fitting solutions to client workflows, and on supportive change management. He recommends small, achievable experiments, while conceding that some people will not adopt. Trust in data privacy is presented as necessary for meaningful use and license uptake. He maintains that lawyers have a standard of care and that strategy and nuance still require people; his reference to AI perhaps being better in thirty years is explicitly uncertain. Shaver's competitive-market observation compares a July 2024 draft with a release less than a year later; her expectation of similar changes elsewhere has no specific deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern law firms, corporate legal and procurement departments, ALSP personnel, technology providers and individual legal professionals, especially those developing AI skills.
pts.d: For corporate legal departments and procurement teams, Tsushima describes faster RFP responses and improved use of existing information repositories. Law firms can benefit from internal knowledge management and procurement applications but face difficulty reconsidering historically profitable billing models. Managing partners accustomed to decades of established practice are portrayed as facing a particularly difficult transition. Lawyers gain faster document processing while retaining professional responsibility and some verification work. Morae, identified by Tsushima as an ALSP with a consulting and professional-services core, seeks to differentiate its managed services by providing AI-skilled attorneys who can also help clients develop internal capabilities. Legal engineers and people skilled in prompting are described as increasingly sought after across firms, corporate departments and ALSPs. Tsushima says younger technology-forward attorneys may be more inclined to adopt, but that prior technology experience cuts across age groups; he also describes privacy practitioners as more inclined toward AI than litigators. He predicts that junior lawyers may leave employers that restrict familiar tools, while employees who champion AI may strengthen their organizational position. For technology providers, multi-model architectures offer adaptability, and Shaver's account identifies new contract-review vendors as increasingly credible competitors to established products such as Kira and Luminance. The source does not provide a concrete claim about access to justice or unmet public legal need.
